title: Should you text more? - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Cowen highlights a Nature panel study of 1,966 US adults finding little credible evidence that use of ten social technologies predicts later life satisfaction; between people, texting correlates with higher satisfaction while YouTube and TikTok correlate with lower.

insights.claim: A five-wave panel of 1,966 US adults found little credible evidence that use of any of ten common social technologies predicts subsequent life satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Weakens the evidentiary basis for social media harm regulation affecting platform companies.
insights.quote: there is scant evidence of a meaningful relationship between social technology use and subsequent life satisfaction
insights.locator: Here, in five waves of panel data

insights.claim: Across people, frequency of texting is associated with higher life satisfaction, while frequency of YouTube and TikTok use is associated with lower life satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Cross-sectional reputational risk for short-video platforms vs messaging.
insights.quote: frequency of texting was associated with higher life satisfaction, whereas frequency of YouTube and TikTok use was associated with lower life satisfaction

insights.claim: Increases in life satisfaction predicted only modest increases in video calling in select demographic groups.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Reverse causation is weak; usage is not driven much by wellbeing shifts.

insights.claim: The study's ability to detect within-person change was limited by temporal stability in responses, though the absence of cross-lagged effects is still informative.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Caveat on how strongly to lean on null result.
